note: Clean pass with one disclosed deviation: item_text ships the canonical MFQ30 wording (moralfoundations.org MFQ30.doc, July 2008) rather than the study .sav's own variable labels, because those labels are an abridgement (Part 1 drops 'Whether or not '; MATH and GOOD carry the depositor's '[use this to cut...]' scoring notes). The labels are what ties code to text and they reconcile 32/32 to the shipped sentences. Note for data users: MATH and GOOD are the MFQ30's two catch items and belong to no foundation subscale, so a five-foundation score computed over all 32 live items would be wrong.

Pass with caveats. (1) instructions and section_prompt are left blank: the study administered the MFQ30 twice, once for the self and once as a prediction of how a typical member of the opposite gender would respond, and the reworded stereotype-condition prompts are not published in the paper, its S1 Appendix (informed-consent form only) or the S1 File .sav. Shipping the canonical MFQ30 Part 1/Part 2 prompts here would have shipped self-referential text ('...relevant to your thinking?') that this table's respondents did not read. (2) Part 1 option_text ships the six short anchors only; the canonical form's first-person parentheticals on the 0 and 5 anchors ('This consideration has nothing to do with my judgments of right and wrong' / 'This is one of the most important factors when I judge right and wrong') were omitted for the same reason, and the paper's own description gives only the short endpoint labels. (3) STP_MATH and STP_GOOD are the MFQ30's two catch items (the .sav labels them 'someone was good at math[use this to cut if >2]' and 'It is better to do good than to do bad[use this to cut if <3]'); they are shipped with their canonical wording and the bracketed screening annotation stripped. (4) Rights: no restriction on the MFQ wording is quotable. moralfoundations.org/questionnaires invites reuse -- 'If you are a researcher and you want to collect data yourself, please use the MFQ30' and 'Want to translate the MFQ into your language? Please do!' -- and MFQ30.doc itself carries no terms, only an attribution line. The site footer's bare 'Copyright 2024 by MoralFoundations.org. All rights reserved.' is a copyright notice, not a reserved-right clause (the PANAS case). Paper is CC BY 4.0.

Pass with caveats. Study 1 randomly assigned participants to an English- or a Spanish-language version of the identical task (63 English, 56 Spanish of the 119 analysed; the debriefing screen states "we randomly assigned different people to do the tasks with either Spanish or English instructions"). The shipped item_text/section_prompt is the English administered wording; the Spanish equivalents administered to the other 56 are, verbatim from the Spanish slide deck: learning-phase item prompt "¿Qué objeto acabas de ver?" and test-phase item prompt "¿Qué objeto es uno de los 6 objetos aprendidos?". The instruction-language condition is recorded in the deposit's Part1_means.csv (`instruct` column) but was NOT carried into the IRW response table, so a user cannot tell which participant read which. `language` and the *_translated columns are deliberately omitted: English is one of the two administered languages, not a substitute for an unrecovered original.

item_text is the literal on-screen prompt, which is identical for every trial within a phase: "Which object did you just view?" on the 18 learning-phase trials of each block and "Which object is one of the 6 target objects?" on the 54 test-phase trials. The stimuli themselves are images of novel objects (Greebles/Sheinbugs/Ziggerins) with no text, so there is no per-trial wording to transcribe and none was invented.

`instructions` is left blank. The only whole-session framing text was shown in the unscored practice block that precedes item 301 ("PRACTICE / Memorize the object in the next 3 images. A test will follow." and "PRACTICE / Which object did you just view? There is only 1 correct answer. Click on the correct object."); it belongs to no scored item, so it is recorded here rather than shipped as table-wide instructions.

Discrepancy between paper and administered slides, disclosed rather than reconciled: the paper says the learning phase "used the same format and instructions" as the practice trials, i.e. the three-sentence prompt above. The actual English and Spanish slide decks show only the single sentence "Which object did you just view?" on learning-phase trials; the extra two sentences appear on PRACTICE screens only. The slides are the administered material and were transcribed.

The item blocks are NOT in presentation order. Participants did Ziggerins, then Greebles, then Sheinbugs (paper, Measures), but the response columns are 1xx = Greebles, 2xx = Sheinbugs, 3xx = Ziggerins -- confirmed against Table 1's per-task M/SD (see verify_nomt_hooper_2024_study1.R; pooled deviations 0.000/0.000/0.003 vs 0.123 under presentation-order labelling) and against the deposit's own Part1_means.csv header "Greebles(100),shein(200),ziggs(300)". section_prompt therefore attaches the first-test framing to the 3xx block, not the 1xx block.

option_text labels the 0/1 accuracy scoring ("Incorrect"/"Correct"), which the paper states outright ("each item was scored as 0 (incorrect) or 1 (correct)"). The three response alternatives a participant actually clicked were object images with no text, so no option wording exists. correct_response is blank for the same reason: the slide filenames encode which of the three screen positions was correct, but the IRW resp is accuracy, not the chosen position.

Rights: no restriction locatable on the NOMT wording. The deposit (figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.24395098) and the article (Behav Res Methods, PMC11685244) are both CC BY 4.0, the study authors created the Spanish version themselves, and the shipped strings are generic task prompts printed verbatim in the CC BY article. No fee, no-redistribution or non-commercial clause found to quote; NOMT is not in instrument_rights_register.csv.
